d1: A plume fixed in the mantle while the Pacific plate slides over it, printing a chain of volcanoes that gets older to the north-west — the clearest ruler we have for plate motion.
The only place a mid-ocean ridge rises above sea level, held up by a plume beneath the spreading Atlantic.
The North American plate riding south-west over a plume, leaving a track of calderas across the Snake River Plain.
A plume beneath the equatorial Pacific whose islands are young enough that their species are still visibly diverging.
The plume that erupted the Deccan Traps, still burning under the Indian Ocean 66 million years later.
Three rifts meet over a plume here; two are opening the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, the third is splitting Africa itself.
The plume that erupted the Parana-Etendeka basalts and then wrote its track across the seafloor as the Walvis Ridge while the South Atlantic opened.
A plume that built one of the largest oceanic plateaus on Earth, and briefly gave the southern Indian Ocean a drowned micro-continent with forests on it.
A long Pacific seamount chain, the southern counterpart to Hawaii's track.
A South Atlantic plume with a distinctive deep-mantle chemical signature.
A Pacific plume whose islands rise steeply from deep water with almost no reef fringe.
A plume close to the East Pacific Rise; the interaction between the two builds an unusually broad volcanic ridge.
A plume sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, thickening the crust and lifting the islands above the sea.
A slow-moving plume off north-west Africa; because the African plate barely moves over it, the islands stay volcanically active far longer than Hawaii's.
A plume beneath one of the largest swells on the ocean floor, raising the seabed more than two kilometres.
A chain of volcanoes running from the Atlantic onto the African continent -- unusually, it crosses the ocean-continent boundary without a break.
Volcanism in the central Sahara that built mountains rising from the desert to over three kilometres.
The southernmost active volcano on Earth, holding a permanent lake of molten lava through the Antarctic winter.
A plume near a triple junction in the South Atlantic, and the most remote island on the planet.
A southern Indian Ocean plume; iron shed from its islands fertilises one of the largest plankton blooms in the world.

vw: Still visible, but draw it as a LAVA PLAIN, not a highland. The crust sagged into the space vacated as the lava rose, so the Columbia 'Plateau' is really a slightly depressed basin; the topographic highs are the Yakima folds, not the basalt surface itself.
d1: The youngest continental flood basalt province, laid down across the Pacific Northwest as the Yellowstone plume arrived beneath the continent.

vw: The Ethiopian Highlands ARE the flood basalt pile - the surface is almost entirely above 1,500 m and culminates at Ras Dashen, 4,550 m. The Main Ethiopian Rift now bisects it.
d1: Flood basalts over the Afar plume that domed up East Africa and began tearing it open — the rifting still going on today.

vw: The most intact silicic LIP landform on Earth: 1,500 x 240 km broadly above 1,800 m, reaching ~3,340 m, with the Barranca del Cobre cut deeper into it than the Grand Canyon. Welded ignimbrite is at least as durable as basalt.
d1: The largest silicic volcanic province on Earth: ignimbrite sheets across northern Mexico, erupted as the subducting Farallon slab rolled back and the crust above it began to tear open into the Gulf of California.

vw: Revised to 0 - the remnants ARE landforms, even though the Thulean plateau as a whole was split and drowned by the rift it caused. East Greenland preserves up to 2.5 km of basalt over 65,000 km2, the Faroes a ~6 km succession reaching 882 m, and Antrim ~3,086 km2. Iceland is new crust, not preserved 62 Ma plateau.
d1: Eruptions as Greenland and Europe parted. Carbon released here is a leading suspect for the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, the sharpest warming of the Cenozoic.

vw: About 500,000 km2 of the original ~1.5 million km2 survives - roughly a third - still over 2 km thick, and its western edge IS the Western Ghats escarpment: 900-1,500 m of relief running ~1,600 km, rising to Anamudi at 2,695 m.
d1: Vast basalt flows across western India, erupting as the subcontinent drove north over the Reunion plume. Their peak brackets the Chicxulub impact, and the two together ended the Cretaceous.

vw: Survives as coastal strips (Androy, Mailaka, Analalava). Crucially, Madagascar's central highlands are Precambrian basement, NOT the 88 Ma basalts - so this province is not the island's defining relief and should not be drawn as such. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Eruptions as Madagascar separated from India, leaving the island isolated — and its life to evolve alone.

vw: The oceanic plateau that stops being a plateau. Its crust is 10-20 km thick, straddling the ~17 km threshold below which plateaus subduct normally, so its margins were obducted onto Colombia, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Curacao while the interior was trapped in an enclosed basin and smoothed flat by terrigenous fill. Still thickened crust; no longer bathymetric relief. LOW CONFIDENCE on the date.
d1: A thick oceanic plateau that proved too buoyant to subduct; it jammed between the Americas and became the floor of the Caribbean.

vw: Still the largest and thickest oceanic plateau on Earth: 1.5-1.86 million km2, crust 33 km, crest ~1,700 m against a 4,500-5,000 m abyssal floor. Draw it WHOLE - over 90 percent is intact. It did not subduct; it jammed the Vitiaz trench and forced a subduction polarity reversal, with only the SW margin deforming and slices obducted onto Malaita and Santa Isabel.
d1: The largest oceanic plateau on Earth, erupted onto the floor of the Pacific in a few million years. It helped push the mid-Cretaceous into an extreme greenhouse and starved the oceans of oxygen.

vw: 770,000 km2 with a crest at 2,500-3,000 m and crust 21-25 km thick; rifted from Ontong Java Nui.
d1: One of three fragments of Ontong Java Nui, a single Cretaceous mega-plateau that a spreading triple junction later split apart.

vw: Still a plateau but the most damaged of the three: ~400,000 km2 survives of an original ~800,000. It jammed the Chatham Rise at ~100 Ma and is now partly subducting beneath the North Island, imaged 37-140 km down.
d1: The third fragment of Ontong Java Nui. Too buoyant to sink easily, it is now jamming into the subduction zone beneath New Zealand.

vw: The Alpha Ridge carries 38 km of crust - thicker than Ontong Java - with 2,700 m of relief and a crest at ~1,250 m. Worth splitting in the renderer: Alpha and Mendeleev ridges submarine, Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Ellesmere subaerial.
d1: Magmatism spanning the Arctic as the Amerasia Basin opened, from Svalbard to the Sverdrup Basin and the Alpha Ridge.

vw: After CAMP, the best example of a giant province that is not a landform. Its main surviving record is reworked volcanic detritus in the Eromanga and Great Artesian basins; Coral Sea rifting at ~62-52 Ma removed most of the rest.
d1: A vast silicic province along eastern Australia. Unusually for a province this size it is driven by slab rollback rather than a mantle plume.

vw: Only ~4,100 km2 is exposed against ~200,000 km2 buried under the Bengal Basin - about 2 percent visible. Killed by burial, not erosion: the rock is fine, the landform is gone.
d1: The Kerguelen plume's first arrival under eastern India, before the plate carried the continent onward.

vw: The Brazilian Serra Geral remains a major plateau and escarpment; Etendeka is a much smaller severed remnant. Split by South Atlantic opening, with the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise marking the join.
d1: One province split in two: its halves now sit in Brazil and Namibia, torn apart by the opening South Atlantic.
A large igneous province: flood basalts erupted over a geologically brief interval, on a scale with no modern equivalent.

vw: Ignimbrite plateaus of the Deseado Massif and the Antarctic Peninsula still stand with moderate relief after 150 Myr, though much is buried under the Austral-Magallanes and San Jorge basins. LOW CONFIDENCE - not verified against a primary source.
d1: One of the largest silicic provinces known, erupted across Patagonia and the Antarctic Peninsula as the Weddell Sea began to open.

vw: Ceased to be a plateau when it accreted, but survives in a way no other province does: it kept its full 25-30 km crustal thickness (usually accretion strips plateaus to 8-15 km) and is now the Wrangell-St Elias Mountains, Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii. Accretion age genuinely spans 160-100 Ma in the literature. Caveat: its exposed section includes subaerial flows, so it may never have been a classic deep-ocean plateau.
d1: An oceanic plateau erupted in Panthalassa and later rammed into North America, where it now forms a belt of accreted crust from Vancouver Island to Alaska. It is the leading suspect for the Carnian Pluvial Episode.

vw: The oldest surviving oceanic plateau, and empirical proof that isostatic relief outlasts thermal subsidence: Tamu Massif's summit is at ~1,980 m against a ~6,400 m base, giving ~4,460 m of relief after 145 Myr, on 26 km of crust.
d1: A huge Pacific plateau built at a three-way junction of spreading ridges. Whether a plume or the junction itself made it is still argued.

vw: The key negative result, and the largest province by area (~11 million km2) with almost no topographic legacy at all. It was never a plateau: Newark Basin flows are sandwiched between lacustrine formations, buried by rift-basin subsidence within ~100,000 years of eruption; the Amazonian sills were emplaced at depth; the Moroccan basalts survive precisely BECAUSE they were buried. The Palisades cliffs are an intrusion exhumed in the Pleistocene, not a preserved lava surface. Show CAMP erupting and then vanishing almost at once - that is what actually happened.
d1: Magmatism spread across four continents as Pangaea began to split, opening the crack that became the Atlantic. It coincides with the end-Triassic extinction.

vw: The Putorana Plateau is the surviving high ground, 800 x 500 km with Mount Kamen at 1,678 m and the classic trap step-topography intact after 252 Myr on cold, dead craton - the longest-surviving flood basalt landform of the Phanerozoic bar Kalkarindji.
d1: The largest continental flood basalt known: perhaps four million cubic kilometres of lava across Siberia in under a million years, and — as it burned through coal and evaporite — enough carbon and sulphur to acidify the oceans and drive the end-Permian extinction, the worst in Earth's history.

vw: Over 250,000 km2 survives - about half - up to 5.5 km thick. But note the modern Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau elevation is Cenozoic and Tibet-related: the basalt is resistant caprock on a young plateau, re-exhumed, not a continuously surviving Permian landform.
d1: Flood basalts in South China, associated with the end-Guadalupian extinction some eight million years before the far larger end-Permian crisis.

vw: Only 105 km2 of lava flows are exposed today. Pillow lavas and hyaloclastites show partly submarine emplacement, followed by progressive thermo-tectonic subsidence of the Indian passive margin. The modern Pir Panjal elevation is Neogene Himalayan tectonics re-using old rock, NOT a surviving Permian landform - correcting an easy misreading.
d1: Flood basalts in Kashmir that rifted the Cimmerian terranes off Gondwana and opened the Neotethys Ocean behind them.

vw: Largely buried under Tarim Basin sediment, cropping out only at the Keping and Bachu uplifts. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Early Permian magmatism beneath what is now the Tarim Basin, erupted through the heart of central Asia.

vw: Preserved as dyke swarms and sills around the Oslo Rift and Skagerrak; the volcanic edifice did not survive Permian-Triassic rifting and burial.
d1: Late Carboniferous magmatism across northern Europe as Pangaea finished assembling and the crust behind the collision began to pull apart.

vw: Mostly buried under the Dnieper-Donets and Pripyat basin fills; the Kola alkaline complexes survive as intrusive roots only.
d1: Late Devonian rift volcanism across the East European craton, close in age to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

vw: Dismembered and buried by the accretionary tectonics of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt.
d1: Devonian plume volcanism in central Asia, erupted through the collage of arcs and terranes that would become Siberia's southern margin.

vw: A small sill-and-volcanic province caught up in the Verkhoyansk fold belt; no primary landform survives.
d1: Ordovician magmatism on the Siberian platform, roughly contemporary with the great diversification of marine life.
Magmatism on the eastern Siberian craton around a billion years ago, at the far edge of this reconstruction.

vw: Dominantly the Vilyui and Chara-Sinsk dyke swarms plus basalts buried under the Vilyui Basin. LOW CONFIDENCE.
d1: Late Devonian flood basalts that tore open the eastern Siberian platform, and the leading candidate for the Frasnian-Famennian extinction that removed most reef-building life.

vw: If confirmed, the record-holder for flood-basalt landform longevity at ~511 Myr: the Antrim Plateau Volcanics sit on arid, stable Australian craton, the single most favourable preservation setting there is. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE - verify against a primary source before shipping, since a 511 Myr surviving landform is a strong claim.
d1: Australia's Cambrian flood basalts, linked to an early-Cambrian extinction pulse not long after animals first diversified.
Rift volcanism as Rodinia's fragments finally separated and the Iapetus Ocean opened between them.

Enormous eruptions across what is now Arctic Canada at the threshold of the Sturtian glaciation. Weathering of fresh basalt in the tropics is thought to have drawn down enough CO2 to help freeze the planet.
Rift magmatism along the edge of Laurentia as Rodinia began to come apart, well before the supercontinent finally broke.
Early Neoproterozoic dyke swarms across Australia, marking the first tearing of Rodinia's interior.
Plume magmatism beneath the South China block during Rodinia's breakup, in the run-up to the Cryogenian glaciations.
Dykes and sills across the joined Sao Francisco and Congo cratons, erupted as Rodinia stretched after assembling.
A dyke swarm across the Pilbara of Western Australia, and one of the anchor points for reconstructing where Australia sat within Rodinia.
The rift that is currently splitting Africa. Projected forward, it floods and becomes an ocean.
Projected volcanism where Africa drives into Europe and the Mediterranean closes, raising a mountain chain along the suture.
Projected arc volcanism along the closing ocean between the converging continents of the future supercontinent.
A dyke swarm across the North China craton, and the likely conjugate of the Bahia- Gangila dykes in South America and Africa -- evidence for how those blocks were joined a billion years ago.
Bimodal volcanism on the Yangtze craton, part of the long sequence of eruptions that accompanied Rodinia's breakup in South China.
One of a series of magmatic pulses beneath South China as Rodinia came apart, feeding the rift basins that later filled with glacial debris.
One of the largest silicic provinces of the Precambrian: rhyolites and granites across Rajasthan, erupted as Rodinia stretched. Its rocks record where India sat inside the supercontinent.
Magmatism on the southern edge of the Siberian craton, proposed as a continuation of the Franklin event and so as part of what tipped Earth into the Sturtian glaciation.
A dyke swarm in southern Africa of the same age as the Franklin eruptions in Arctic Canada, on the other side of a world about to freeze over.
Ediacaran flood basalts across what is now Ukraine, erupted as Baltica pulled away from the rest of Rodinia -- and close in time to the first large, soft-bodied animals.
A deep-crustal magmatic province in Arctic Norway, emplaced as the Iapetus Ocean began to open. What is exposed is its plumbing, not its volcanoes.

vw: Buried under the Anadarko Basin, then partly exhumed as the Wichita Mountains during the Pennsylvanian - a re-exposed root, not a surviving plateau.
d1: Cambrian rift volcanism and layered intrusions along a failed arm of the opening Iapetus. Buried for 300 million years, then shoved back into daylight as the Wichita Mountains when Pangaea assembled.

vw: Sills near the Lena mouth, incorporated into the Verkhoyansk belt.
d1: Cambrian sills near the mouth of the Lena, erupted at roughly the same time as Australia's Kalkarindji basalts on the far side of the world.

vw: Deformed into the Alborz range during Cimmerian and later collisions.
d1: Ordovician volcanism along the northern edge of Gondwana, and one of very few candidates in a stretch of time otherwise almost empty of large igneous provinces.

vw: Dolerite sills armour the Transantarctic Mountains the length of the range, preserved by polar-desert conditions for 183 Myr.
d1: The Antarctic half of the Karoo-Ferrar event: dolerite sheets injected the length of the Transantarctic Mountains, whose dark banded cliffs are this magma frozen in place.

vw: Carried into the Himalayan collision zone and deformed; no plateau survives, only tectonised basalt and dykes in southern Tibet.
d1: The Kerguelen plume's opening act on the Gondwanan side, now folded into southern Tibet -- carried half the world from the province it was erupted with.

vw: A small but intact Late Jurassic Pacific plateau - among the oldest surviving seafloor topography anywhere.
d1: A small Late Jurassic plateau, and one of the oldest surviving pieces of seafloor topography anywhere on the planet.

vw: Largely buried under the Perth Basin's Cretaceous-Cenozoic fill.
d1: The Australian half of the Kerguelen plume's arrival, erupted just before the continent tore away and now buried beneath the Perth Basin.
The southern twin of the Tristan plume. The two built the Walvis Ridge together and then separated into distinct chemical lineages -- evidence that a single plume can be striped.

vw: A broad guyot-capped rise; the flat tops record subsidence from sea level, so it was once an island chain and is now a drowned one.
d1: A broad Cretaceous rise whose volcanoes once broke the surface as islands with coral reefs; they have since subsided into flat-topped seamounts drowned a kilometre down.

One of the longest hotspot tracks on Earth, running from the Monteregian Hills of Quebec through the White Mountains and the New England Seamounts to a drowned volcano in the mid-Atlantic. North America slid clean over it.

vw: The main body of a 1.23 million km2 edifice rising 2,000 m above the surrounding basins. Note it was LAND: ODP recovered fossil wood, charcoal- bearing soils and river-transported clasts, and at its peak this was an island of ~500,000 km2 with peaks 1,000-2,000 m above sea level. Final drowning ~20 Ma.
d1: The main body of a drowned volcanic continent a third the size of Australia. Cores drilled from it contain wood and coal -- it had forests before it sank.
A South Pacific plume whose track can be followed back through the Cook-Austral chain into the Tuvalu, Gilbert and Marshall islands -- possibly the oldest hotspot still erupting in the Pacific.

vw: Buried beneath the Bengal Basin's Himalayan sediment load; only the Shillong Plateau margin still exposes it.
d1: The eastern twin of the Rajmahal Traps, erupted in the same pulse over the Kerguelen plume and now buried under the sediment of the Bengal delta.

vw: Strongly asymmetric: crest at ~2,161 m in the south deepening to 4,637 m in the north. Vesicular non-pillowed trachyte flows show it was probably above sea level early in its history.
d1: A mid-Cretaceous plateau on the Pacific floor, built while the ocean was making new crust faster than at any time since. Its lavas erupted into air, not water -- it stood above the sea before it sank.

vw: Still bathymetrically prominent, with Heard Island (Mont Ross, 1,850 m) and the Kerguelen archipelago emergent above it.
d1: The middle segment of the Kerguelen edifice, built as the plume continued to feed the growing plateau after India had moved on.

vw: 300,000 km2 standing 2.5 km above the surrounding seafloor with a summit at 2,500 m depth and crust 20-25 km thick.
d1: A basalt plateau south of Africa, erupted as the last threads between Africa and Antarctica parted. It still rises two and a half kilometres above the surrounding seafloor.

vw: The Antarctic third of the same 1.2 million km2 plateau, whose relief still steers the Weddell Gyre and opens the recurring Weddell Polynya.
d1: The Antarctic counterpart of the Agulhas Plateau, split from it as the Southern Ocean opened. Its bulk still steers the currents above it, opening a recurring hole in the winter sea ice.

vw: A shallow bathymetric ridge in the eastern Indian Ocean, rifted off the Central Kerguelen Plateau in the Eocene; its flank stood ~2,000 m above sea level at the moment of rifting.
d1: The rifted-off northern edge of the Kerguelen Plateau, carried away when a spreading ridge cut the plateau in two during the Eocene.
The plume that split Madagascar from India and erupted the Madagascar flood basalts, leaving the island alone in the Indian Ocean with its own evolutionary experiment.
A plume beneath the South Atlantic that first surfaced inland, erupting diamond- bearing kimberlites across Brazil before the continent carried on west and left it offshore.
A chain of seamounts in the central Indian Ocean, and one of the harder features to reconcile with a fixed-plume model.
A slow plume off Iberia whose track runs north-east along the Tore Rise; like the Canaries, it stays active because Africa barely moves.
A plume that never built a chain but lifted a broad swell of seafloor. Bermuda itself is a single drowned volcano capped by limestone.

vw: The youngest and shallowest segment, carrying the Kerguelen Islands.
d1: The youngest segment, still fed by the plume and still carrying islands above water in the far southern Indian Ocean.
A South Atlantic plume near the ridge, one of a cluster whose chemistry samples the edge of the African deep-mantle pile.
The most active volcano in the Austral chain, a seamount that occasionally boils the sea surface without ever quite breaching it.
A north-east Pacific plume whose seamount chain runs into the Juan de Fuca Ridge, where plume and ridge have been interacting for tens of millions of years.
A hotspot Australia has been sliding over for thirty million years, leaving the longest continental volcanic track on Earth -- a line of dead volcanoes from Queensland to Victoria.

vw: The conjugate half of the same 30 Ma plateau, severed by Red Sea and Gulf of Aden opening and now standing as the Yemen highlands.
d1: The other half of the Afar flood basalts, erupted at the same moment as the Ethiopian Traps and then torn away from them as the Red Sea opened. The two plateaus now face each other across the water.
A western Pacific plume whose track runs through the Caroline Islands and carries some of the ocean's deepest-rooted volcanic chemistry.
A plume off Chile whose islands are carried east toward the trench, where the ridge it built jams into the Andean subduction zone.
A plume beneath West Antarctica, feeding volcanoes that erupt through the ice sheet and melt it from below.
A small Atlantic plume off north-east Brazil, its islands the eroded necks of volcanoes that never grew large.
A plume in the Tasman Sea whose oldest island has eroded to a spire of rock rising six hundred metres straight out of the ocean.
A Pacific plume with an unusual twist: it sits beside the tearing corner of the Tonga trench, which pulls its magma sideways.
A Gulf of Alaska plume whose seamount chain bends north toward the Aleutian trench, mirroring the Hawaiian track on a smaller scale.
A hotspot that printed a line of seamounts down the Tasman Sea while the Australian plate raced north over it.
A southern Pacific plume whose seamount chain runs from near the East Pacific Rise toward the Tuamotus.
A plume between Africa and Madagascar; its newest volcano grew from the seafloor off Mayotte within the last decade, and was detected by the earthquakes it made on the way up.
A young Pacific plume whose islands are so isolated they were the last refuge of the Bounty mutineers.
A plume beneath French Polynesia, building the high volcanic islands that subside into the ring-shaped atolls Darwin explained.

The asteroid that ended the Cretaceous. A ten-kilometre body struck the Yucatan shelf, throwing enough rock and sulphur into the atmosphere to darken and chill the planet for years, and taking the non-avian dinosaurs with it.
A Siberian crater whose impact shocked graphite into diamond across the surrounding rock. It falls in a late Eocene cluster of strikes.
A Late Triassic crater, its ring-shaped lake now one of the most recognisable features from orbit.
An Ediacaran impact in South Australia. Its ejecta layer sits in rocks alongside some of the earliest complex organisms.
A Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary crater buried under the Kalahari, found only by its magnetic signature.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 65 km across, formed about 70.7 million years ago.
One of the oldest large craters in North America, its structure dismembered and scattered by later mountain building.
An Early Cretaceous impact into a shallow Australian sea, now buried under the Eromanga Basin.
An Ordovician crater on the St. Lawrence; the modern river follows the weakened rock around its rim. Long dated to the Carboniferous, it was reassigned to ~450 Ma by U-Pb on shocked zircon.
A Devonian crater in Sweden, the largest in Europe, its ring of lakes still visible in the landscape.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 52 km across, formed about 25.0 million years ago.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 45 km across, formed about 51.1 million years ago.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 141.0 million years ago.
A late Eocene strike on the North American shelf; the buried crater still steers the modern bay and its groundwater.
Brazil's largest crater, its age falling within uncertainty of the end-Permian extinction, though it is far too small to be its cause.
A crater on the floor of the Barents Sea, which triggered a tsunami across the shallow Jurassic seaway.
A buried Devonian crater in Western Australia, near in age to a major extinction pulse.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 40 km across, formed about 227.8 million years ago.
A large Early Jurassic structure on the Russian platform, now almost entirely buried.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 39 km across, formed about 481.5 million years ago.
The larger of the two Clearwater lakes. The pair look like a classic double impact, but their ages differ by nearly 200 million years -- they are unrelated.
An Iowa crater once proposed as the killer of the dinosaurs, until redating placed it about ten million years too early.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 646.0 million years ago.
Buried under a kilometre of the Greenland ice sheet and found by radar. It is far older than the ice: when it formed, the target was rainforest.
An archipelago in Lake Superior that is the central uplift of an Ordovician crater, its rocks full of shatter cones.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 28 km across, formed about 37.8 million years ago.
The smaller Clearwater lake, and the older by far. Its Ordovician age is what disproved the twin-impact story its shape suggests.
An Arctic crater recognised only in 2010, its rim visible from the air as a ring of disturbed strata.
Confirmed as an impact structure only in 2025, after shatter cones were found around a ring-shaped basin spotted on satellite imagery.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 25 km across, formed about 50.4 million years ago.
A Miocene crater in Bavaria. Its ejecta scattered glass across central Europe, and the town of Nordlingen is built inside it.
A Ukrainian crater that struck roughly 650,000 years AFTER Chicxulub, into a world still recovering from it. Its lake sediments record that recovery in fine detail.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 206.9 million years ago.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 77.9 million years ago.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 22 km across, formed about 142.5 million years ago.
A confirmed impact structure roughly 23 km across, formed about 31.0 million years ago.
